cards.text: Many years later, Artaxerxes is king of Persia, and we meet a man named Ezra. His family line runs son after son, all the way back to Aaron the chief priest. Friend, I showed up with a 25-cent price sticker, and this man shows up with a FAMILY FOREST.

cards.question: Ezra comes up from Babylon. He's a scribe, skilled in the Law of ___.
Ezra brings his requests to the king of Persia, and the king says yes to ALL of them. How does a scribe from Babylon pull that off?

answers.text: The hand of the LORD was upon him
The queen of Persia spoke for him
The elders of Judah stood with him

cards.text: Cut to the seventh year of King Artaxerxes. Ezra's bags are packed, and he's headed up to Jerusalem.

cards.question: Ezra makes the trip up to Jerusalem all by himself.

cards.text: Ezra leaves Babylon on the first day of the first month and arrives in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month. Left on the FIRST, showed up on the FIRST, friend, and I can't even get a batch out on the day I planned.

cards.question: So Ezra's trip from Babylon to Jerusalem takes ___ months.

cards.text: FOUR MONTHS on the road, and I get antsy waiting on a ten-minute oven timer! He made it, because "the gracious hand of his God was upon him."

cards.question: Ezra set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, then leave living it out to everybody else.
Ezra set his heart to study the Law of the LORD and to practice it. What's the third thing he set his heart to do?

cards.text: Now we get the actual letter King Artaxerxes gave Ezra, and he opens by calling himself "king of kings." Friend, my whole title is a name somebody carved into my handle.

cards.question: In the king's letter, only the priests and Levites are allowed to go up to Jerusalem with Ezra.

cards.text: The king AND his seven counselors are sending Ezra off with a job to do. Seven counselors! The only second opinion I get around here is from the oven.

cards.question: Ezra is sent to evaluate Judah and Jerusalem according to the ___ of his God.

cards.text: Then comes the money. Ezra carries silver and gold the king and his counselors FREELY offered to the God of Israel, plus silver and gold from the province of Babylon and freewill offerings from the people and priests.

cards.question: With all that silver and gold, what does the king tell Ezra to buy?

answers.text: Animals to offer on the altar
Stone and timber for the walls

cards.question: Whatever silver and gold is left over, Ezra has to send back to the king.

cards.text: Ezra must deliver to the God of Jerusalem all the articles given for the service of His house, and anything else the house needs, Ezra may pay for from the ROYAL TREASURY. Friend, nobody has EVER said that about my chocolate chip bill.
Then King Artaxerxes writes to all his treasurers west of the Euphrates about whatever Ezra the priest may require of them. I bet those treasurers got REAL quiet reading this one.

cards.question: Whatever Ezra requires, how quickly must the treasurers west of the Euphrates provide it?

cards.text: The treasurers must give up to a hundred talents of silver, a hundred cors of wheat, a hundred baths of wine, a hundred baths of olive oil, and salt without limit. Salt WITHOUT LIMIT, friend, and here I am counting my sprinkles.

cards.question: King Artaxerxes says whatever the God of heaven commands must be done diligently for His house. What reason does the king give?

answers.text: So wrath won't fall on his realm and sons
So the people will keep paying their taxes
So his own name is honored in Jerusalem

cards.question: The treasurers can still charge tribute and tolls to the priests, Levites and other servants of God's house.

cards.text: Then the king turns to Ezra himself, a man who has the wisdom of his God, and hands him a job bigger than any cookie box I ever packed.

cards.question: Ezra is to appoint ___ and ___ for all the people west of the Euphrates who know the laws of his God.

cards.text: Ezra is also to teach these laws to anyone who doesn't know them, and whoever won't keep the law of Ezra's God and the law of the king faces strict judgment. That letter is NOT a suggestion box, friend.

cards.question: The king's letter is done, and now Ezra speaks for himself. Who does Ezra bless for putting it into the king's heart to honor God's house in Jerusalem?

answers.text: The LORD the God of his fathers
The governor west of the Euphrates

cards.text: Ezra says the LORD showed him favor before the king, his counselors and all the king's powerful officials. With the hand of the LORD his God upon him, Ezra took courage and gathered the leaders of Israel to return with him. Grab a cookie for the road, friend, because this story is NOT done.

findings.problem: The passage opens with "Many years later," which continues from the previous passage. The opening card repeats "Many years later" without saying what it is later than (the temple being finished in Ezra 6). It also never says what is going on, which is Ezra coming up from Babylon to Jerusalem. The third sentence is spent on a joke, so the baker gets the genealogy but no setting.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: This story card is three sentences: "The king AND his seven counselors are sending Ezra off with a job to do." / "Seven counselors!" / "The only second opinion I get around here is from the oven." Only the opening card may run to 3 sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This story card is three sentences: the favor before the king, the courage and gathering of the leaders, and then the line saying the story isn't over. It also carries more than two beats. Trim or merge the retelling so the card stays within 2 sentences, including the closing line.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The right answer "Promptly" is a single word. Both wrong answers are three words ("Within a year" and "After a review"), so the right answer stands out by its length.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "governors" is close in meaning to the right answer "magistrates". Both are civil officials appointed over people, so a baker could argue that "governors" fits the blank.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The setup on card 14 only says Ezra gets "a job bigger than any cookie box," and the question removes "to judge" from the verse. That leaves the baker guessing the exact title "magistrates" rather than reasoning out the meaning of the job, which is appointing people to judge.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.
